title: The importance of the human urge to move

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As any fan of the Olympic Games knows, people can get very excited about a race to see who the fastest man or woman is over a particular distance. Yet from a certain point of view, it’s strange that the physical prowess of humanity should be cause for celebration at all. By the standards of the rest of the animal kingdom, the performance of even the top 100-metre sprinter is nothing to shout about. Is it not baffling that the athletics elite should receive adulation when it’s in the mental sphere that our species genuinely excels?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But such thinking neglects the enormous influence of the drive to move on the evolution of Homo sapiens, an influence that extends far deeper than the famous freeing of our hands and their opposable thumbs* that occurred when our ancestors became full-time bipeds. Indeed, the opposable thumb itself likely evolved as an adaptation to safe movement in the trees tens of millions of years before our forebears left the trees for the savannah. But more importantly, our psychology is still adapted for a life on the move, even in the least energetic among us. Understanding the mechanism behind this may help us to live more joyful lives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most well-known psychological movement-driver is surely the runner’s high – a sense of well-being and euphoria that can be engendered by long-distance running. These emotions used to be attributed to endorphins, but we now know that chemicals called endocannabinoids are largely responsible. Named after their resemblance to the active ingredient of cannabis, endocannabinoids are powerful pain-killers that additionally cause the release of the neuromodulator dopamine in the brain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dopamine is usually described as a reward chemical, whose evolutionary function is to give us an emotional hit when engaged in activities which improve our species’ long-term prospects. The runner’s high makes perfect sense in this light. Our African ancestors probably used a persistence hunting technique – running after their animal prey for hours until it dropped from exhaustion – as do some hunter-gatherers today. A dopamine boost was undoubtedly vital in maintaining the required pace.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Unfortunately for many of us, a high level of aerobic fitness is a necessary precondition of the runner’s high. Attempting a prolonged run without it causes a build-up of lactic acid in our bodies, leading to muscle ache, burning, rapid breathing, nausea and stomach pain long before the endocannabinoids kick in, and we just feel grim. However, there are gentler ways of using movement to get a dopamine hit.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are a range of techniques which can be used to find out exactly how dopamine’s emotional bribery works. One such technique carried out on research subjects is called fast-scan cyclic voltammetry. It uses electric currents delivered through carbon-fibre electrodes inserted into the brain to measure changing dopamine concentrations over split-second timescales. Another technique is optogenetics, which lets a researcher alter an active animal’s dopamine levels. It does this by first infecting the animal with a virus which has been genetically engineered and causes dopamine-secreting cells to become light-sensitive. These cells can then be controlled with flashes of light in implanted optic fibres. Such techniques were recently used by researchers at the University of Michigan to see how dopamine influences the behaviour of rats. The rats in question were trained to carry out what was essentially a treasure hunt: a sequence of movements guided by visual and auditory cues, which if followed correctly, resulted in the delivery of food. The research showed that the dopamine concentration in the brain increased sharply every time a rat registered a cue and embarked on the next stage of the sequence. If the dopamine concentration was artificially increased using fibre optic implants, the rats showed a greater propensity to begin the hunt, and learned the meaning of the cues more rapidly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Michigan results tell us that dopamine’s role is more complex than was once thought. Rather than acting as a general reward, it appears to be a specific motivator of motion. But motion alone is not enough. The correlation between dopamine release and the presentation (and learning) of unexpected cues indicates that active exploration is the key stimulator of its release. The Michigan results suggest that you don’t have to be a distance runner to experience the dopamine high. Walking will do as long as it’s used to explore the surroundings, so full sensory engagement is a must. This will come as no surprise to hunter-gatherers: it’s what they do all the time, and many anthropologists have noted the emotional benefits they draw from their wanderings. But in our developed world with its cars and sat-navs, getting out of our cars and just exploring is increasingly regarded as pointless, and most of us seriously underestimate the pleasure that the simple act of movement might bring.
